segments.title: Judge frigates by the missions they must perform
segments.summary: The opening replaces a simple best-ship ranking with a comparison of mission, force role, and the level of combat each design must survive.
segments.body: A warship's value depends on the job its navy expects it to do. River-class offshore patrol vessels illustrate the point: they suit presence, diplomacy, and maritime security, while a high-threat battle would demand a different ship. A modern frigate can support a screen and perform picket duties, although a destroyer is more likely to be built as the task group's principal screening asset. Light frigates occupy another tier because their cost, weapons, and wartime assumptions differ from those of larger frigates. The comparison therefore follows the requirements that produced each class instead of trying to name one universal winner.

evidence.note: The introduction defines the comparison by mission and contrasts OPVs, light frigates, frigates, and destroyer screening roles.

segments.title: Type 26 as a specialist submarine hunter
segments.summary: Type 26 is an expensive ASW specialist built to defend task groups against equally costly and capable submarines.
segments.body: Type 26 begins with a clear purpose: finding and killing submarines before they can attack a task group. Submarines are dangerous because they can approach unseen, yet history also shows that dedicated surface and air ASW forces can destroy them. The escort must protect troop transports, supply ships, and carriers whose combined value far exceeds the frigate's own price. That requirement explains why a first-rate submarine hunter cannot be treated as a cheap platform. Rafted machinery, hull shaping, sensors, and accumulated ASW experience all serve the same specialist mission.

evidence.note: The lecture identifies Type 26 as an ASW specialist and links its cost and design measures to the submarine threat.

segments.title: City, River, and Hunter variants in allied task groups
segments.summary: The British, Canadian, and Australian Type 26 variants adapt one ASW-centered design to different assumptions about task-group support and coalition service.
segments.body: Every Type 26 variant must defend itself and contribute outside ASW, even though submarine hunting remains its foundation. The Royal Navy's City class can rely on carrier-group aircraft and Type 45 destroyers for much of the outer air-defence battle. Canadian River-class destroyers and Australian Hunter-class frigates face a broader integration problem because they may join British, American, Japanese, or other allied formations. Their wider sensor and weapon fits help them reinforce both ASW and air defence when the composition of the allied formation changes. Canada may also use its large planned River force in surface action groups. The variants show how coalition expectations can reshape a common hull without erasing its original purpose.

evidence.note: The passage compares City, River, and Hunter requirements and explains how each variant fits national and allied task groups.

segments.title: Type 26 as the task group's ASW director
segments.summary: Type 26 is meant to coordinate a task group's ships, aircraft, and uncrewed systems as well as hunt submarines with its own sensors.
segments.body: Type 26 is cast as the ASW equivalent of the air-defence ship that directs a task group's wider defensive picture. Its own sensors and quieting give it first-rate hunting ability, while its larger role is to coordinate other ships and aircraft. Uncrewed systems extend that network under the frigate's direction. This arrangement brings separate search assets into one submarine-hunting effort across the formation.

evidence.note: The lecture compares Type 26 with an air-defence director and says it should see and direct the task group's ASW assets, including uncrewed systems.

segments.title: How Type 26 is arranged around ASW sensors
segments.summary: The flight deck, mission bay, sonars, computing spaces, and quiet propulsion plant reveal how deeply ASW shapes the Type 26 layout.
segments.body: The weapons occupy a limited part of the layout, while the stern carries a large flight deck, hangar, and mission bay for crewed or uncrewed ASW assets. The discussed British fit lacks the dedicated shipboard torpedo launchers often expected on an ASW frigate; such launchers would normally fire the same class of lightweight torpedo carried by the helicopter. Hull form keeps the flow around the bow-mounted Type 2150 sonar as clean as possible. The Type 2087 towed array can search farther away and share a wider detection picture with other ships and aircraft. Computer space, cooling, and electrical power matter because modern ASW depends on combining several streams of acoustic data. Rafted machinery and electric motors reduce the ship's own noise. Quieting also makes the frigate harder to detect, while its primary benefit here is allowing the sonars to hear weak submarine signatures through less self-generated interference.

evidence.note: The lecture connects the mission bay, aviation facilities, Type 2150 and Type 2087 sonars, computing, and quiet propulsion to the ASW mission.

segments.title: FREMM modularity and the Constellation redesign problem
segments.summary: FREMM offers an adaptable base design, while Constellation shows how national substitutions can turn small interface changes into a major redesign.
segments.body: FREMM was conceived as a modular, adaptable frigate family that customers could configure for different mission mixes. That flexibility still assumes users will work with the interfaces and modules built into the design. The US Constellation program is used as the cautionary example because American equipment choices required new power, intake, and internal arrangements. Even equipment of a similar physical size can force cables, ducts, cooling, and foundations to move. A series of individually modest substitutions can therefore propagate through the hull until the adapted ship becomes a much larger engineering project.

evidence.note: The passage introduces FREMM modularity and explains how changed equipment interfaces accumulated in the Constellation redesign.

segments.title: FREMM trades some ASW specialization for breadth
segments.summary: Type 26 concentrates on ASW, while FREMM accepts a lower peak in that specialty to remain useful across a wider set of missions.
segments.body: FREMM retains a strong ASW capability, but its French and Italian requirements spread design effort across more jobs. A rough comparison rates Type 26 as a 90 percent ASW solution and FREMM as a 75 to 80 percent solution that can also reach about 70 percent across other missions. Those figures are illustrative judgments rather than test scores. They explain why a navy seeking one balanced ship may prefer FREMM, while a force with separate air-defence and strike assets can afford a more focused Type 26. Portugal is given as an example of a customer that needs a broad, practical capability from each hull.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts Type 26 specialization with FREMM's broader French and Italian general-purpose requirements.

segments.title: Why FREMM attracted so many national variants
segments.summary: A useful core hull, adaptable mission fit, and credible independent capability made FREMM attractive to navies with very different patrol and combat needs.
segments.body: FREMM can patrol dispersed territories, support fire missions, hunt submarines, contribute to air defence, and enter contested waters without needing an entire task group beside it. The Italian variants make that flexibility especially visible through their layered weapons. At the time of the comparison, plans had reached 66 ships across several customers, followed by 27 French and American cancellations, with 22 hulls active. Orders were still evolving, so the figures describe a program snapshot rather than a final class total. The design's appeal comes from a sound common base that can accept different national priorities. Conceptually, it is a higher-end development of the MEKO approach to modular warship families.

evidence.note: The passage covers FREMM mission breadth, national orders and cancellations, and its relationship to modular design families such as MEKO.

segments.title: FREMM weapon layers, firing arcs, and redundancy
segments.summary: The Italian FREMM fit introduces a wider design lesson: limited magazines expose earlier threat assumptions, while overlapping gun arcs and redundant layers keep defensive options available.
segments.body: In this interpretation, Type 26 and FREMM reflect an era when Western navies expected technological superiority and more freedom to choose their wars. Their limited VLS capacity and uneven defensive layers still carry that assumption, although the Italian FREMM fit closes more of the gaps. It combines missiles, a five-inch gun, 76 mm guns, and 25 mm weapons so threats can be engaged at several ranges. Layering also provides alternatives when one system fails or exhausts its ammunition. Two mounts with restricted arcs may leave an entire side uncovered after a casualty, while three or four mounts preserve useful overlap. Guns and future laser systems need an unobstructed line of sight, so their positions should be fixed early. Vertical-launch missiles can turn after launch, giving designers more freedom to place their cells once the direct-fire arcs are protected.

evidence.note: The lecture uses Italian FREMM layers to explain system availability, overlapping coverage, firing arcs, and VLS placement.

segments.title: Project 17 frigates for independent Indian operations
segments.summary: Shivalik, Nilgiri, and the planned Project 17B form an iterative frigate family shaped by India's need to operate without assuming allied support.
segments.body: Project 17 develops through the Shivalik class, Project 17A Nilgiris, and the planned Project 17B ships. Indian planning begins with the expectation that the navy may have to operate alone, while allied help remains useful when available. That assumption pushes each frigate toward a flexible mix of self-defence, task-group support, and offensive reach. The ships can reinforce carrier or surface groups and also conduct visible deployments across the Indian Ocean and farther abroad. Each generation reduces acoustic, infrared, and other signatures while increasing capability. The line has also moved from Indianized versions of Russian design ideas toward a recognizable national style, strengthening the ships' value for overseas presence.

evidence.note: The passage traces Project 17 development and links Indian frigate design to independent operations and wider power projection.

segments.title: Project 17B weapons and defensive depth
segments.summary: The planned 8,000-ton Project 17B anchors a discussion of BrahMos, Barak 8, 76 mm guns, AK-630 mounts, and RBU-6000 launchers as a layered Indian fit.
segments.body: Project 17B is planned as an approximately 8,000-ton third iteration with about 48 vertical-launch cells. Its planned family capability includes BrahMos anti-ship missiles and the Indian-Israeli Barak 8 air-defence system. The existing gun and close-in fit combines an OTO Melara 76 mm weapon with AK-630 mounts, while RBU-6000 launchers add options in shallow water against submarines or uncrewed threats. The stated AK-630 traverse limits let a mount cover targets around the ship without rotating continuously through a full circle, so crossing its stop may force the gun to slew the long way around. Multiple mounts reduce that delay and preserve an arc if one system fails. Torpedoes and a shipboard helicopter extend the ASW layer. A suggested heavier fit would carry at least 16 BrahMos missiles, 48 Barak weapons, and three each of the 76 mm and AK-630 systems. That recommendation is an opinion about resilience and overlapping arcs; it does not describe the approved configuration.

evidence.note: The lecture gives Project 17B size and VLS estimates, reviews Indian missile and gun systems, and distinguishes the stated fit from a preferred denser armament.

segments.title: Indian ASW helicopters and the cost of learning
segments.summary: A possible Merlin fit leads into the doctrine, onboard computing, and industrial learning needed for India to field an independent ASW helicopter capability.
segments.body: India operates domestically developed helicopters and Sea King variants. An EH101 or new-build Merlin purchase remains an uncertain possibility. A Merlin-sized aircraft may suit an Indian doctrine that gives the helicopter more independence during submarine prosecution. That approach requires more computing capacity and mission equipment aboard the aircraft itself. Russian practice relies more heavily on several aircraft working together, while American helicopters remain closely integrated with their ships. An indigenous replacement would still face the normal mistakes and compromises of a first domestic generation. Licensed production offers one way to learn the design philosophy and manufacturing process before attempting a fully national successor.

evidence.note: The passage compares ASW helicopter operating concepts and explains first-generation indigenous development and licensed-production learning.

segments.title: Three heavy-frigate design philosophies
segments.summary: Type 26 prioritizes ASW, FREMM balances several missions, and the Nilgiri family couples combat capability with growth of India's national naval industry.
segments.body: The three larger frigate families embody different design priorities. Type 26 is the dedicated ASW specialist. FREMM keeps a strong submarine-hunting capability inside a wider general-purpose package. The Nilgiri and Project 17 line adds industrial development, using successive ships to build India's national design and construction base.

evidence.note: The lecture explicitly summarizes Type 26, FREMM, and Nilgiri as products of three different design priorities.

segments.title: Mogami's path from compact destroyer to light frigate
segments.summary: The Mogami program began in 2015 as a compact destroyer effort and settled into a light-frigate role that supplies deployable wartime mass.
segments.body: Japan began the program in 2015 while seeking a new compact destroyer. By August 2026, ten Mogamis are counted as in service, with two more expected before March 2027. That is a rapid construction pace even when the full development period is included. At roughly 4,000 tons standard displacement, the ship falls into the modern light-frigate tier used in this comparison. A patrol vessel handles constabulary work without a frontline warfighting fit, while a corvette is a combatant intended for shorter deployments. A light frigate is the smallest combatant expected to deploy for extended periods and fight within a task group or under land-based cover. Mogami replaces older Asagiri and Abukuma destroyer escorts by adding affordable hulls to larger Japanese formations.

evidence.note: The passage dates the Mogami program, gives its recording-date service count, defines the light-frigate category, and identifies the classes it replaces.

segments.title: Mogami's balanced fit and resistance to feature creep
segments.summary: Sixteen Mark 41 cells, Type 17 missiles, mine equipment, torpedoes, a helicopter, and a five-inch gun give Mogami broad utility without turning it into a larger frigate.
segments.body: Mogami uses a conventional propulsion plant, while its compact integrated mast is singled out as an innovative feature that has attracted interest from India and other navies. Its standard fit includes 16 Mark 41 cells, which could hold 64 quad-packed Evolved Sea Sparrow Missiles or a smaller number of larger weapons. Eight Type 17 anti-ship missiles continue Japan's domestic, iterative missile-development path. Mine-laying equipment, torpedoes, a helicopter, and a five-inch gun cover a wide range of fleet and peacetime work. In role and philosophy, the ship resembles an Oliver Hazard Perry or MEKO 200 updated for current threats. Adding every desirable weapon would quickly increase size and cost, so the existing restraint is part of the design's value.

evidence.note: The lecture reviews Mogami's mast, VLS, missiles, mine and ASW equipment, and the need to control feature growth in a light frigate.

segments.title: Upgraded Mogami missile capacity and Australian choices
segments.summary: The enlarged Mogami doubles Mark 41 capacity to 32 cells, opening different Japanese and Australian choices about domestic missiles, quad-packing, guns, and close defence.
segments.body: The upgraded design rises to about 4,800 tons standard and 6,200 tons fully loaded while retaining similar engine power. Its Mark 41 battery doubles to 32 cells. Japan's Type 23 surface-to-air missile is a domestic option that appears unable to quad-pack, which would limit the number carried once other VLS weapons are included. ESSM and CAMM show how a quad-packed missile could provide much greater defensive depth, whether purchased or developed through international cooperation. The Japanese fit is also expected to retain Type 97 torpedoes and domestic anti-ship missiles. The Australian fit is expected to use ESSM and may add a RIM-116 Rolling Airframe Missile system, with gun choices still discussed. The design remains an adaptable lower-tier escort whose customer can trade domestic content against magazine capacity.

evidence.note: The passage gives upgraded Mogami displacement and VLS figures, then compares Japanese domestic missile and Australian quad-packed options.

segments.title: Mogami supplies mass in Japan's high-low fleet mix
segments.summary: Japan can field affordable Mogamis in numbers because larger Aegis ships cover the top tier and steady yard work lowers the cost of replacing the rest of the force.
segments.body: Japan already has top-tier Aegis destroyers and a middle band of other destroyers, so Mogami can concentrate on the lower escort tier. More hulls spread the formation, provide mutual support, and keep useful ships available in several places at once. Requiring every escort to match a Maya or Kongo would shrink the fleet through cost. The resulting high-low mix balances combat quality with the number of ships needed for routine deployments and wartime depth. Continuous construction also preserves yard skills and avoids the expense of repeatedly restarting production. Australian and other export interest strengthens that industrial logic by extending the run.

evidence.note: The lecture places Mogami in Japan's lower escort tier and connects fleet mass with continuous shipyard production and exports.

segments.title: The uneasy symbolism of HMS Campbeltown
segments.summary: Naming a Type 31 for HMS Campbeltown links the new frigate to amphibious history, although the famous destroyer's deliberate wartime sacrifice makes the choice feel awkward.
segments.body: The Inspiration-class naming scheme is meant to connect each Type 31 with an aspect of Royal Navy history. HMS Campbeltown represents amphibious forces through a destroyer remembered for blowing itself up during an important World War II operation. That act was effective and famous, yet it gives a strange symbolic message to a new ship intended to support amphibious forces. Other raids and participating ships, including those associated with Operation Claymore, offered different naming possibilities.

evidence.note: The lecture questions Campbeltown as an amphibious-forces name and contrasts its wartime sacrifice with other raid histories.

segments.title: Type 31 as the task group's defensive goalkeeper
segments.summary: The British Type 31 fit emphasizes short-range missiles and medium guns, making it a final defensive layer around a carrier or amphibious ship.
segments.body: Arrowhead designs are named for their approximate length, with the Type 31 derived from the Arrowhead 140 family. The British fit functions as a flak frigate or goalkeeper near the carrier or amphibious ship. A 57 mm gun, two 40 mm guns, and a large short-range missile load can engage threats that penetrate the outer screen. Mark 41 cells leave room for strike weapons, although the discussed British emphasis is quad-packed CAMM and local defence. That defensive profile also suits forward presence because it creates a substantial obstacle without presenting the same offensive concentration as a strike-heavy combatant. In a task group, its job is to preserve the protected ship after the longer-range layers have already fired.

evidence.note: The passage explains Arrowhead naming and presents Type 31 as a short-range defensive layer for carriers, amphibious ships, and forward presence.

segments.title: Arrowhead's export appeal is space for adaptation
segments.summary: Polish and Indonesian interest reflects Arrowhead's large hull, moderate crew needs, and room for national weapons and later upgrades.
segments.body: Arrowhead 120, 140, and the discussed 160 variant offer related hull sizes rather than one fixed national fit. Poland and Indonesia can use that space for their own sensors, weapons, accommodation, and future changes. The design is compared with a practical van because the customer receives a sound platform with a large usable interior. Relatively small crews reduce the recurring personnel burden. Efficient construction and open volume make the family attractive to navies that want to shape a ship around their own requirements.

evidence.note: The lecture links Polish and Indonesian interest to Arrowhead hull space, adaptability, crew efficiency, and buildability.

segments.title: How stop-start orders slow British frigate production
segments.summary: British yards can build faster, but changing requirements and too few follow-on orders force slow production that protects workforces at a higher unit cost.
segments.body: Changing government decisions appear to be the main production problem. British yards can assemble ships quickly, but revised requirements may force completed work to be undone and rebuilt. Slow funding then stretches a small order so the yard does not finish years before the next program is ready. Full-rate Type 26 production could absorb Norwegian ships with less disruption, but the workforce would face a sharp fall once the run ended without enough successor work. Uncertainty around the former Type 83 plan illustrates how that gap can reappear. Regular orders would let yards build faster while retaining the people and facilities needed for the next class.

evidence.note: The passage connects British schedule changes, low order volume, Norwegian Type 26 slots, and workforce continuity to slow, costly production.

segments.title: StanFlex, MEKO, and two kinds of modularity
segments.summary: The Iver Huitfeldt lineage contrasts StanFlex's rapid in-service module swaps with MEKO's more commercially successful design-stage customization.
segments.body: Arrowhead builds on the capable Iver Huitfeldt design and its Danish experience with StanFlex. StanFlex modules can be craned off and replaced quickly, allowing a ship to change equipment after entering service. Denmark retained the concept but sold it poorly abroad. MEKO succeeded with a different promise: customers begin with a common core design and choose modules while the ship is being designed and built. Other attempts at rapid in-service reconfiguration have struggled despite strong interest in modular language. Light frigates would benefit most from genuine mission changes because their numbers and internal space could support mine warfare, amphibious support, or maritime-security packages as requirements shift.

evidence.note: The lecture compares StanFlex module swaps, MEKO design-stage customization, and the unrealized value of in-service modularity for light frigates.

segments.title: FDI combines combat utility with visible presence
segments.summary: FDI offers a more purposefully integrated light-frigate package whose striking silhouette also serves French presence and export aims.
segments.body: Vehicle analogies separate the three light-frigate approaches. Type 31 is the spacious van, Mogami is the flexible estate car, and FDI is the more purposefully arranged saloon. Mogami reduces radar signature through conventional stealth shaping, while FDI also creates an unmistakable visual identity. That visibility supports port visits and global French presence because observers can recognize the ship immediately. Combat utility remains central, and the distinctive silhouette gives the ship additional status. That combination helps explain why other navies see FDI as a route to fleet capability and a prominent national presence.

evidence.note: The passage uses vehicle analogies to distinguish Type 31, Mogami, and FDI, then links FDI's visual character to presence and export value.

segments.title: French, Greek, and Swedish FDI missile fits
segments.summary: One FDI hull supports markedly different French, Greek, and Swedish missile magazines, ranging from compact Aster fits to mixed CAMM, Aster, and strike-length cells.
segments.body: The French baseline uses two eight-cell Sylver A50 launchers for 16 Aster 15 or Aster 30 missiles. The final two French ships are expected to gain another 16 cells for a total of 32. Sweden's Luleå variant is planned with 24 CAMM-ER weapons and 24 Aster 30s, creating a 48-missile air-defence load. The Greek configuration carries 24 Aster cells and another eight A70 cells for land-attack cruise missiles. A50 is the tactical-length launcher, while A70 provides the longer strategic cell. These differences show how one compact hull can be adapted around national ideas of local air defence, Baltic operations, and strike capability.

evidence.note: The lecture compares French, Swedish, and Greek FDI missile-cell counts and distinguishes Sylver A50 and A70 lengths.

segments.title: FDI gun fits, order totals, and French program cost
segments.summary: National gun choices sit beside a small total order of 13 FDIs and a French program estimate of about 700 million euros per ship including development.
segments.body: The French and Greek versions use the OTO Melara 76 mm gun, while Sweden keeps its Bofors tradition with 57 mm and 40 mm weapons. Plans at the time total five French, four Greek, and four Swedish ships. That produces only 13 hulls despite the design's export success. The five-ship French program is estimated at about 3.5 billion euros including development, or roughly 700 million euros per ship in 2025 money. Construction accounts for 2.1 billion euros and development for 1.4 billion, so comparisons need to separate recurring hull cost from one-time design expense.

evidence.note: The passage lists national gun fits, planned hull totals, and the French construction and development cost breakdown.

segments.title: FDI as a Baltic principal combatant and export demonstrator
segments.summary: Sweden can use its FDI-derived frigates as principal Baltic combatants, while France demonstrates how an in-service ship can strengthen diplomacy and export campaigns.
segments.body: Swedish FDI-derived ships are expected to act as principal surface combatants in the Baltic, especially because the navy will operate only a small number. A recognizable and visibly capable ship can carry diplomatic weight when it enters a port or appears during a regional operation. France has reinforced that effect by sending an in-service FDI to visit potential customers and demonstrate the design. Greece's Kimon also gives buyers a second operational national variant to examine. Being able to tour and inspect a working ship can change how procurement teams judge a design. Mogami and FDI have gained an advantage in competitions where they could appear in service while Type 31 remained a paper or building-stage offer.

evidence.note: The lecture identifies the in-service French Amiral Ronarc'h and Greek Kimon as tangible examples that can be shown to potential customers.
The closing comparison links Swedish Baltic duties and warship appearance with French and Japanese use of in-service ships during export campaigns.
